input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Detail the baseline linear prompting comparator and the graph-aware prompting system variants evaluated. List implementation details to report (model family or API used, prompt templates, JSON schema enforcement, evidence-retrieval mechanism, and key generation hyperparameters). State any ablations or alternate schedules compared and note computational budget and randomness controls (e.g., seeds) insofar as space permits.

output:
We compare the proposed graph-aware prompting pipeline against a straightforward linear prompting comparator and evaluate several ablations of the graph-aware system. Below we describe the treatment arms used in experiments, the class of implementation details we record for reproducibility, the prompt and schema conventions enforced during generation, and the controlled sources of randomness and compute reporting used in our study.

Baseline and system variants
- Linear prompting baseline: a pipeline that writes sections in document order (from introduction toward conclusion) using the same evidence retrieval interface and the same JSON output schema as the experimental systems. The baseline omits any explicit section dependency graph or leaf-first scheduling and therefore synthesizes high-level sections without guaranteed prior synthesis of dependent subsections.
- Graph-aware (full): the full proposed pipeline that (1) constructs a document graph of section/subsection dependencies, (2) schedules generation in a leaf-first ordering derived from the graph, (3) injects ranked evidence snippets and provenance for each section at generation time, and (4) enforces JSON-constrained outputs that include required citation entries.
- Graph-aware ablations and alternates: to isolate which components drive observed differences we evaluate the following variants:
  1. Graph-aware without JSON enforcement — identical to the full system but with schema conformance checks disabled at generation time (schema checks retained only during post-hoc validation).
  2. Graph-aware with breadth-first scheduling — replaces leaf-first ordering with a breadth-first traversal of the section graph to test ordering effects.
  3. Graph-aware with limited evidence scope — restricts retrieval to only locally scoped notes for each section, testing sensitivity to retrieval scope.
  4. Linear + schema enforcement — baseline linear order but with the same JSON output schema enforced to quantify the isolated effect of schema constraints.

Recorded implementation details for reproducibility
For every experimental run we record the following configuration items and make them available in the artifact appendix:
- model endpoint or family and API parameters (e.g., model identifier, decoding temperature, maximum generation length);
- exact prompt templates (instruction text, examples, placeholders) used for each section type and for each system variant;
- JSON output schema specification and the enforcement mechanism (inline prompting constraints, post-generation validator, or both);
- evidence retrieval backend and index composition (index sources, passage granularity), the query formulation policy used per section, and the snippet-ranking heuristics applied before injection;
- generation and retrieval randomness controls (random seeds where APIs permit deterministic sampling, and the seeding strategy used for retrieval ranking);
- hardware and computational budget accounting (compute devices used, wall-clock time per run, and aggregate resource consumption) reported in the supplement.

Prompting and schema conventions
- Prompt structure: all prompts for experimental runs follow a small number of standardized blocks: (i) a concise task specification describing required section content and the JSON schema to produce; (ii) injected evidence snippets with explicit provenance tags; (iii) formatting instructions that require inclusion of citation markers tied to provenance entries; and (iv) failure-handling instructions that direct the model to produce an explicit ``INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE'' field when no supporting snippet can be found.
- JSON schema: the schema requires fields for a section title, a short structured outline, the prose body, and a list of cited sources (each with a provenance id and short locator). For the full system the generator is prompted to emit only schema-conformant JSON; for ablations this enforcement is removed or relaxed as stated above.
- Evidence injection: prompts present ranked snippets with provenance immediately prior to the generation instruction; generators are instructed to place inline citation markers that reference the provenance identifiers and to avoid asserting factual claims that are unsupported by the provided snippets.

Randomness controls and compute reporting
- To reduce run-to-run variance we fix random seeds for any controllable components (retrieval sampling, decoding where supported by the API). Where deterministic seeding is not possible due to external API constraints, we report observed variance across repeated runs.
- We report computational resource usage (hardware type, number of parallel generator instances, and cumulative wall time) in the supplementary materials to enable cost comparisons across variants.

Notes on scope and limitations
- The section-level experimental design and the precise implementation choices (model identifiers, hyperparameter values, and retrieval index contents) are documented in the appendix and accompanying artifact to enable exact replication. Where platform restrictions prevent deterministic reproduction (for example, closed-model APIs that do not allow fixed seeds), we explicitly flag these limitations alongside the reported results.
